Suzent must already be running. `--no-require-auth` disables pairing and chat
isolation for trusted local integrations. See [editor setup](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/nodes#use-suzent-from-your-editor-acp).

See [Use Suzent from your editor](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/nodes#use-suzent-from-your-editor-acp).

## For developers

`suzent start --dev` and `suzent restart --dev` run Suzent from a source
checkout in development mode, and `suzent update --dev` updates that checkout
to the latest development version. `suzent logs --frontend`
reads the development window's log, and `suzent setup-build-tools` installs
the Windows build tools needed to compile the desktop app. See the
[development guide](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/contributing/development-guide).

`suzent chats read <chat_id> --offset 0 --limit 20` reads a page of visible messages
without assistant reasoning traces. Use the returned `next_offset` to continue;
`null` means there are no more messages.

`suzent chats show <chat_id>` prints a conversation from its file in
`~/.suzent/chats/`. `suzent chats verify` checks that the index in `chats.db` matches every
conversation file in `~/.suzent/chats/`, and lists any that do not.
`suzent chats rebuild-index` rewrites every conversation in `chats.db` from
those files; quit Suzent before running it. See
[chat storage](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/chat-storage).


---

# Configuration files

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/configuration




Almost everything can be changed in **Settings**, and that is the easiest way.
This page is for the settings that have no screen yet, and for knowing where
your files are. Your memory, skills, and settings are plain files you can read,
edit, and back up.

## The data folder

Suzent keeps your data in a `.suzent` folder in your home folder: `~/.suzent`
on macOS and Linux, `C:\Users\<you>\.suzent` on Windows. To keep it somewhere
else, set the `SUZENT_DATA_DIR` environment variable before starting Suzent.

| Path | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `config/` | Your settings files (see below). |
| `chats/` | Your conversations, one plain-text file each. This is the master copy. |
| `chats.db` | An index of your conversations, plus your projects, tasks, and schedules. Suzent rebuilds the conversations in it from `chats/` if it goes missing. |
| `sandbox/projects/<project>/` | Each [project's library](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/filesystem#where-files-go). |
| `sandbox/shared/` | The folder shared by all projects. Your memory's Markdown files are in `sandbox/shared/memory/`. |
| `notebook/` | The [notebook](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/memory/llm-wiki) vault. |
| `memory/` | The memory search index, rebuilt from the Markdown files. |
| `skills/` | Skills you added. See [Skills](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/skills). |
| `runtime/` | Logs. `server.log` is the background service's log. |
| `github-sync/` | The local copy used by [GitHub Sync](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/github-sync). |
| `browser_profile/` | The agent's own browser profile, when it remembers logins. |

API keys are not kept in these files. Suzent stores them in your system's
keychain, or in an encrypted `secrets.db` in this folder when no keychain is
available.

## The Suzent folder

A few files live in the folder Suzent is installed in (`~/suzent` if you
installed with the terminal script), not in the data folder:

| File | What it holds | In the app |
|---|---|---|
| `.env` | Environment variables read when the server starts, such as `SEARXNG_BASE_URL`. | |
| `config/social.json` | Chat app connections and allowed users. `config/social.example.json` shows every option. | **Settings → Social Channels** |

## Settings files

These are in `~/.suzent/config/`:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `default.yaml` | Your own settings, for anything without a screen in the app. Synced by GitHub Sync. |
| `local.yaml` | Settings that only make sense on this computer, such as folder paths. Never synced. |
| `config.yaml` | Preferences the app saves for you. Let the app manage it. |
| `permissions.yaml` | Your "always allow" rules and the default permission mode. See [Permissions & approvals](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/human-in-the-loop#where-rules-are-kept). |
| `permission-audit.jsonl` | A log of every permission decision. |
| `skills.json` | Which skills are switched on or off. |

Suzent reads its settings in this order, and a later file wins:

1. `config/default.example.yaml` in the Suzent folder, which ships the defaults.
2. `config/default.yaml` in the Suzent folder, if you made one.
3. `~/.suzent/config/default.yaml`.
4. `~/.suzent/config/local.yaml`.

Keep your changes in `~/.suzent/config/` so updates never touch them. Setting
names are not case-sensitive. Restart Suzent after editing a file.

A list set in a later file replaces the whole list from an earlier one. This
matters for `sandbox_volumes`: choosing a notebook folder in
**Settings → Memory System** writes `sandbox_volumes` to `local.yaml`, and from
then on any `sandbox_volumes` in `default.yaml` is ignored. Keep all your
mounted folders in `local.yaml`.

## Common settings

### Workspace and sandbox

See [Workspace & sandbox](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/filesystem).

| Setting | Default | What it does | In the app |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sandbox_enabled` | `false` | Run commands in a Docker sandbox for every conversation. | **Settings → Security** |
| `sandbox_image` | `python:3.11-slim` | The Docker image the sandbox uses. | |
| `sandbox_network` | `bridge` | `bridge` lets the sandbox use the internet, `none` blocks it. | |
| `sandbox_idle_timeout_minutes` | `30` | Stop a sandbox after this many idle minutes. | |
| `sandbox_setup_command` | `""` | A command run once when a sandbox is created, such as installing packages. | |
| `sandbox_env` | `{}` | Extra environment variables inside the sandbox. | |
| `sandbox_volumes` | | Folders from your computer to mount in every conversation, as `"host folder:path the agent sees"`. Put this in `local.yaml`. | **Settings → Memory System** sets the notebook mount |
| `sandbox_data_path` | `~/.suzent/sandbox` | Where project libraries and the shared folder are kept. Put this in `local.yaml`. | |
| `scratch_max_mb` | `2048` | Size limit for each project's `scratch/` folder. Past it, the oldest files are removed. | |
| `shell_denied_env_patterns` | `[]` | Environment variables hidden from commands the agent runs in host mode, such as `OPENAI_*`. | |

### Memory

See [Memory](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/memory). More tuning is on
[Advanced memory settings](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/memory/configuration).

| Setting | Default | What it does | In the app |
|---|---|---|---|
| `memory_enabled` | `true` | Turn long-term memory on or off. | **Settings → Memory System** |
| `markdown_memory_enabled` | `true` | Write remembered facts to Markdown files. | |
| `embedding_model` | | The model used for memory search. | **Settings → Model Roles** |
| `extraction_model` | | The model that picks out facts to remember. | **Settings → Model Roles** |
| `notebook_dir` | `~/.suzent/notebook` | Where the notebook vault is kept. | |
| `memory_consolidation_enabled` | `true` | Let Suzent tidy memory into the notebook in the background. | |
| `memory_lint_enabled` | `true` | Let Suzent audit the notebook for contradictions and broken links. | |
| `lancedb_uri` | `~/.suzent/memory` | Where the memory search index is kept. Put this in `local.yaml`. | |

### Conversations

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `max_context_tokens` | `0` | Cap the context budget. `0` uses whatever the model supports. |
| `context_compaction_trigger` | `0.80` | How full the context gets before older messages are summarized. |
| `goals_max_turns` | `20` | How many turns [goal mode](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/automation#goal-mode) runs before pausing. |
| `session_daily_reset_hour` | `0` | UTC hour at which conversations reset each day. `0` turns it off. |
| `session_idle_timeout_minutes` | `0` | Reset a conversation after this many idle minutes. `0` turns it off. |
| `stream_idle_timeout_seconds` | `120` | How long to wait between model response updates when the provider has no default of its own. Tool execution has separate limits. |
| `stream_wait_notice_seconds` | `15` | Show a waiting notice after this many seconds without a model response update. You can still stop the response. |
| `stream_wait_slow_seconds` | `60` | Show a slow-response notice and offer more waiting time. |
| `stream_wait_extension_seconds` | `1200` | Maximum silence allowed after you choose Continue waiting, counted from the last response update. Choosing it again does not add more time. |
| `stream_idle_timeout_overrides` | `{}` | Override response waiting times, in seconds, by provider ID or full model ID. A model override takes priority. Google Gemini's provider default is 300 seconds. |

For example, add this to `local.yaml` to allow a provider 10 minutes between
response updates, with a longer wait for one model:

```yaml
stream_idle_timeout_overrides:
  gemini: 600
  gemini/gemini-4-argon: 900
```

All waiting times must be positive, finite numbers. These settings do not change
the time allowed for tools or the separate first-response waiting policy.

### Devices and other agents

See [Devices & other agents](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/nodes). The app saves these in
`local.yaml`.

| Setting | Default | What it does | In the app |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node_lan_bind` | `false` | Let other devices on your network reach this computer. Takes effect after a restart. | **Settings → Mesh → Network access** |
| `node_discovery_enabled` | `true` | Announce this computer on your network so other devices can find it. | |
| `a2a_enabled` | `false` | Publish a card so other A2A agents can find this device. | **Settings → Mesh** |
| `a2a_agent_name` | `""` | The name on that card. Blank uses the computer's name. | **Settings → Mesh** |

### Permissions

`default_permission_mode` in `permissions.yaml` sets the mode new
conversations start in: `default` (**Ask**), `auto` (**Smart**), or
`full_access` (**Full Access**). Choosing a mode in a new chat, before its
first message, saves it here.

## Changing settings from the terminal

`suzent config show` prints the settings the running server reports, and
`suzent config set <key> <value>` changes a saved preference such as
`sandbox_enabled` or `memory_enabled`. See
[Command line](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/cli#configuration).

## Environment variables

Set these in your environment before starting Suzent. `SEARXNG_BASE_URL` can
also go in the `.env` file in the Suzent folder.

| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `SUZENT_DATA_DIR` | Use a different data folder instead of `~/.suzent`. |
| `SUZENT_PORT` | The port Suzent's server uses. Default `25314`. |
| `SEARXNG_BASE_URL` | Use your own [SearXNG](https://docs.searxng.org/) instance for web search instead of DuckDuckGo. |
| `SKILLS_DIR` | Extra folders to load skills from. Separate several with `:` (macOS, Linux) or `;` (Windows). |
| `SUZENT_SECRET_BACKEND` | Set to `encrypted_sqlite` to keep API keys in the encrypted `secrets.db` instead of your system's keychain. |
| `SUZENT_BROWSER_*` | Browser options when running without the desktop app. See [Browser](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/browser#running-suzent-from-the-command-line). |

Provider API keys, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`, can also be set as environment
variables. Each provider's page lists its variable; see
[Models & Providers](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/models).


---

# FAQ & troubleshooting

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/faq




## Getting started

### I don't have an API key. Can I still use Suzent?

Yes. [Ollama](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/models/local/ollama) runs models on your own computer
with no key and no internet connection. Google Gemini has a
[free tier](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/models/cloud/gemini), and the
[ChatGPT subscription](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/models/cloud/chatgpt-subscription) provider
signs in with your ChatGPT account instead of a key.

### The terminal says "command not found: suzent".

Close and reopen your terminal after installing. If it still fails, check the
setup script's output for how to add Suzent to your `PATH`. See the
[Quickstart](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/getting-started/quickstart#troubleshooting).

### Suzent won't start because the port is in use.

Suzent uses port `25314`. If an older Suzent is still running, `suzent stop`
ends it. Otherwise start Suzent on another port with `suzent start --port <port>`,
or set `SUZENT_PORT`. See [Command line](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/cli#running-suzent).

### How much am I spending?

Open **Settings → Usage** to see your spending, API calls, and tokens per day.
Type `/status` in a conversation to see that conversation's tokens and cost.

## Your data

### Where are my files?

Everything is in the `.suzent` folder in your home folder. Files the agent
keeps go to the project's library, in `~/.suzent/sandbox/projects/<project>/`.
See [The data folder](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/configuration#the-data-folder) for the full layout.

### Is my data sent anywhere?

Suzent runs on your computer and doesn't send usage analytics. Your messages
go to the model provider you choose, and with Ollama nothing leaves your
machine. Web searches go to DuckDuckGo, or to your own SearXNG. Suzent also
checks GitHub for new releases. GitHub Sync and chat apps only send data once
you set them up.

### How do I back up Suzent, or move to a new computer?

Turn on [GitHub Sync](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/github-sync). It keeps your settings,
skills, and memory in a private GitHub repository you own, and brings them to
another computer. API keys are never synced, so add them again in
**Settings → Providers** on the new computer.

Your conversations are not synced. Each one is a plain-text file in
`~/.suzent/chats/`, so copying that folder keeps all of them. Quit Suzent first
so no conversation is half-written. Put the folder back in a new `~/.suzent`
and Suzent rebuilds your conversations from it on its next start; they appear
in your Home project, because projects themselves are kept in `chats.db`.

### How do I start over from scratch?

To empty a single conversation, type `/clear`. To reset Suzent entirely, quit
it, run `suzent service stop` if you use the background service, then rename
or move the `~/.suzent` folder. Suzent creates a new, empty one the next time
it starts. Your API keys stay in your system's keychain and are picked up again.

### The agent forgot something, or remembers something wrong.

To forget something, delete it in the **Memory** panel. To correct it, say the
corrected version in a conversation. Memory is also a set of Markdown files you
can edit yourself. See
[Managing what's remembered](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/memory#managing-whats-remembered).

## Using the agent

### The agent can't see my folder.

The agent only reaches its project library, the shared folder, and folders you mount. Click
**Working Dir** in the chat box and choose the folder. See
[Giving the agent access to your folders](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/filesystem#giving-the-agent-access-to-your-folders).

### How do I undo what the agent just did?

Click the retry icon under its last reply, or type `/retry`. That rolls back
the last turn, including file edits, and runs your message again. `/undo` only
reverts the file edits. See [Slash commands](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/slash-commands#undo-and-retry).

### Can I stop the agent asking for permission all the time?

Switch the conversation to **Smart** or **Full Access** with the mode selector
next to the message box, or choose one of the
"always allow" answers when it asks. See [Permissions & approvals](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/human-in-the-loop).

### Scheduled tasks don't run when I close the window.

Tasks, heartbeats, and chat apps only work while Suzent is running. Turn on
**Settings → Background Service** to keep it running after you close the
window. See [Automation](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/automation#keep-suzent-running-in-the-background).

## Troubleshooting

### My chat app bot doesn't reply.

Check three things. Suzent must be running, so turn on the background service
if you closed the window. The app must be enabled in
**Settings → Social Channels**. And your own user ID must be in
**Allowed users** on the **Access control** tab, because messages from anyone
else are refused. See [Access control & pairing](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/chat-apps/access-control).

### The sandbox won't start.

The sandbox needs Docker. Make sure Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine on Linux)
is running, and that `docker ps` works in a terminal. To work without it, turn
the sandbox off in **Settings → Security**. See
[Using the sandbox](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/filesystem#using-the-sandbox).

### Where are the logs?

Run `suzent logs --desktop` for the desktop app's log, and add `-f` to follow
it live. If you use the background service, its log is under
**Settings → Background Service → Service log**, and `suzent service logs`
prints where the file is. All logs are kept in `~/.suzent/runtime/`.

### Something seems broken after installing.

Run `suzent doctor` to check that the tools Suzent needs are installed. For a
background service that won't start, run `suzent service doctor`.

### How do I update?

Open **Settings → About** and click **Check for updates**, or run
`suzent update`. If an update was interrupted, run `suzent repair`. See
[Updating Suzent](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/getting-started/updating).


---

# Settings pages

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/settings




Open **Settings** from the bottom of the left sidebar. Pages are grouped into
**Agent**, **Connections**, and **Application**.

## All settings pages

| Page | What it's for | More |
|---|---|---|
| **Providers** | Add API keys, sign in to providers, and choose which models are available. | [Models & Providers](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/models) |
| **Model Roles** | Pick which model handles each kind of work, with backups. | [Model roles](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/models/model-roles) |
| **Voice & audio** | Choose how the agent's speech sounds and plays. | [Images, video and speech](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/media) |
| **Memory System** | Turn memory tools on or off, see which models memory uses, and choose the notebook folder. | [Memory](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/memory) |
| **Automation** | Create and manage scheduled tasks, and choose which tools heartbeats may run without review. | [Automation](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/automation) |
| **Social Channels** | Connect Telegram, Slack, Discord, Feishu, or WeChat, and control who may chat. | [Chat apps](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/chat-apps) |
| **MCP Servers** | Add and test servers that give the agent extra tools. | [MCP servers](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/mcp) |
| **Browser** | Choose how the agent connects to a browser. | [Browser](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/browser) |
| **ACP Agents** | Set up coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex to use in chats. | [Working with your agent](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/using/conversations#bring-in-another-coding-agent) |
| **Devices** | Pair your phone and connect other devices. | [Devices & other agents](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/nodes) |
| **Mesh** | Make this computer reachable on your network, and work with other agents. | [Devices & other agents](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/nodes) |
| **Appearance** | Theme, color scheme, and language. | [Making it yours](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/using/make-it-yours#look-and-language) |
| **Background Service** | Keep Suzent running after you close the window. | [Automation](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/automation#keep-suzent-running-in-the-background) |
| **Security** | Turn the sandbox on for every chat, and create host tokens for remote administration. | [Workspace & sandbox](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/filesystem), [Permissions & approvals](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/human-in-the-loop) |
| **Data & Sync** | Sync your settings, skills, and memory through GitHub. | [GitHub Sync](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/github-sync) |
| **Usage** | See what you've spent and how many tokens you've used. | [FAQ](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/faq#how-much-am-i-spending) |
| **About** | Version information and updates. | [Updating](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/getting-started/updating) |

Permission modes and approval rules aren't on a settings page. You set the mode
per chat, under the message box, and save rules as you answer requests (see
[Permissions & approvals](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/human-in-the-loop)).

### In the web console

When you use Suzent in a web browser instead of the desktop app, settings
pages are listed in the console's own sidebar. Two pages work differently
there:

- **Browser** isn't shown.
- **Background Service** is replaced by **Operations**, which shows the
  background service's status, lets you restart it, and shows its log.


---

# Slash commands

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/slash-commands




Type a slash command as a message, starting with `/`. Suzent handles it
directly instead of sending it to the model. In the desktop app, typing `/`
in the message box shows the commands available there, and `/help` lists them
anywhere.

The **Works in** column uses these names:

- **Desktop**: the chat in the desktop app or web browser.
- **Chat apps**: Telegram, Slack, Discord, Feishu, and WeChat. See
  [Chat apps](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/chat-apps).
- **Terminal**: `suzent agent chat`. See [Command line](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/reference/cli#chatting-from-the-terminal).

A command typed where it doesn't work is sent to the agent as an ordinary
message.

## Conversation

| Command | What it does | Works in |
|---|---|---|
| `/help` (also `/h`, `/?`) | List the commands available here. | Everywhere |
| `/status` (also `/stat`) | Show Suzent's health, plus this conversation's model, context use, tokens, and cost. | Everywhere |
| `/model` | Show the model this conversation uses. | Everywhere |
| `/model ls` | List your enabled models. | Everywhere |
| `/model <model-id>` | Switch this conversation to another model. Part of a name is enough if it matches only one model. | Everywhere |
| `/compact [focus]` | Summarize the conversation so far to free up context. Add text to say what the summary should focus on. | Everywhere |
| `/clear` (also `/reset`) | Clear this conversation's history so new messages start fresh. | Desktop, Terminal |
| `/fork` | Make an independent copy of this conversation. In a chat app, you are switched to the copy. | Everywhere |

## Undo and retry

| Command | What it does | Works in |
|---|---|---|
| `/retry` | Roll back the last turn, including files the agent changed, and run your message again. The retry button under the agent's reply does the same. | Everywhere |
| `/retry-edit <text>` | Like `/retry`, but runs `<text>` instead of your original message. Editing your last message in the desktop app does this. | Everywhere |
| `/undo` | Undo the file changes from the agent's last turn, without rerunning it. It stops if a file was changed again since then. | Everywhere |

Only the last turn can be undone. Changes made by shell commands aren't rolled
back. See [Undoing the last turn](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/filesystem#undoing-the-last-turn-retry).

## Goals

Goal mode keeps the agent working across turns until an objective is met. See
[Goal mode](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/automation#goal-mode).

| Command | What it does | Works in |
|---|---|---|
| `/goal <objective>` | Set a goal. The agent starts working on it right away. | Everywhere |
| `/goal` or `/goal status` | Show the current goal and its progress. | Everywhere |
| `/goal pause` | Pause the goal. | Everywhere |
| `/goal resume` | Resume it with a fresh turn budget. | Everywhere |
| `/goal clear` | Remove the goal. | Everywhere |
| `/subgoal <text>` | Add a condition that must also be met. | Everywhere |
| `/subgoal` | List the extra conditions. | Everywhere |
| `/subgoal remove <N>` | Remove condition number N. | Everywhere |
| `/subgoal clear` | Remove all extra conditions. | Everywhere |

## Chat apps only

These commands exist because a chat app has no buttons for switching
conversations or answering a permission request.

| Command | What it does | Works in |
|---|---|---|
| `/approve [id]` (also `/y`, `/yes`, `/allow`) | Approve the action the agent is waiting on. | Chat apps |
| `/ya` | Approve it and remember the answer for the rest of the conversation. | Chat apps |
| `/deny [id]` (also `/n`, `/no`, `/reject`) | Refuse the action. | Chat apps |
| `/new [title]` | Start a new conversation and switch to it. | Chat apps |
| `/sess ls` | List your conversations. | Chat apps |
| `/sess switch <id>` | Switch to another conversation. | Chat apps |
| `/sess new [title]` | Same as `/new`. | Chat apps |
| `/sess info` or `/sess` | Show the current conversation. | Chat apps |

In the desktop app and the terminal, you answer permission requests when they
appear instead. See [Permissions & approvals](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/tools/human-in-the-loop).

## Devices

| Command | What it does | Works in |
|---|---|---|
| `/node list` | List connected devices. | Desktop, Terminal |
| `/node status` | Show device connectivity. | Desktop, Terminal |
| `/node describe <device>` | Show what a device can do. | Desktop, Terminal |
| `/node invoke <device> <command>` | Run one of a device's commands. | Desktop, Terminal |

See [Devices & other agents](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/nodes).


---

# Agent Communication

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/agent-inbox




Suzent treats every agent-backed conversation as an addressable session. The
stable `agent_id` is its chat ID; `kind` describes how the session originated:
`interactive`, `subagent`, `cron`, or `social`.

## Tools

| Tool | Parameters | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `agent` | task definition and execution options | Creates a child agent |
| `agent_list` | `status`, `limit` | Lists accessible sessions in the current project |
| `agent_read` | `agent_id` | Reads a bounded, visible transcript |
| `agent_send` | `agent_id`, `message`, `wait` | Queues a durable message and wakes the target; `wait=True` runs the target's turn now and returns its reply |
| `agent_stop` | `agent_id` | Cooperatively stops an active target |

The project is the authorization boundary. Hidden internal sessions (dream and
legacy wakeup chats) are not addressable. Sending to the current session is
rejected to avoid feedback loops.

## Durable Inbox

`agent_send` does not depend on an in-memory queue. It writes an
`agent_inbox_messages` row before returning. A background dispatcher uses a
database lease to claim messages and moves each row through this state machine:

```
pending -> processing -> delivered
              |
              +-> pending (retry with backoff)
              +-> failed  (attempt limit reached)
```

Message IDs are idempotency keys. Delivery also writes a hidden marker into the
target transcript. If a process exits after the target turn commits but before
the inbox acknowledgement commits, the next worker sees the marker and
acknowledges the row without running the target twice.

All local and received peer messages enter the target through the existing
system-reminder format, with sender identity and the delivery marker retained.
Native background turns use `system_reminders`; live-run injection and ACP turns
use a locally authored PUA wrapper with a `display_trigger` for the visible
transcript. Peer transport carries raw message content; the receiver owns its
wrapper and runtime nonce.

Sub-agent completion and failure wakeups use this inbox too, so restarting the
backend no longer discards a completed child's parent notification.

## Following Up With a Sub-agent

A parent continues a finished sub-agent with `agent_send`, addressing it by
task ID or chat ID. The sub-agent's chat stores its role prompt, model, memory
setting, permission mode, and the permission grants it inherited at spawn
(`followup_config`), so the follow-up turn runs as the same sub-agent rather
than falling back to the main agent's prompt, the default model, and none of
the parent's denials. A worktree that teardown keeps becomes the stored working
directory, so follow-ups edit the isolated changes, not the main checkout.

When a delivered `agent_message` came from the target's own parent, the
dispatcher queues the turn's final answer back to the parent as a
`subagent_result` (`subagent-reply-<message_id>`), which wakes it the same way
the first result did. Replies from other sessions stay in their own chat.
If queueing the reply fails, the delivery is retried; the retry finds the turn
already in the transcript, rebuilds the reply from its last answer, and queues
it under the same idempotent ID.
A message that joins a turn already in flight produces no separate reply.

`wait=True` skips the queue: the dispatcher delivers one message at a time, so a
parent waiting from inside a turn the dispatcher is running would wait on
itself. The tool runs the target turn directly and returns the reply, and the
stream layer gives the call no tool timeout, as with a blocking `agent` call.
If the wait is cancelled, the turn keeps running and a sub-agent's reply is
routed back through the inbox. Waited messages are not durable.

## Cron and Social Boundaries

Cron definitions and run records are already durable, but the scheduler invokes
due jobs directly. Its UI announcement deque is still an in-memory presentation
channel; it is not the agent inbox.

Social Brain also keeps a dedicated in-memory ingress queue. Raw social events
carry channel authorization, thread identity, attachments, and reply routing, so
they are validated and normalized by Social Brain before an agent turn. They are
not inserted into the generic inbox. Once normalized, their chat sessions are
visible to `agent_list` and can receive `agent_send` messages like other sessions.

This separation keeps the generic tool contract small while preserving the
special delivery semantics of Cron and social channels.

## Cross-session and Cross-device Semantics

The inbox provides real cross-session communication. Paired Suzent backends are
also exposed as remote agent addresses such as `peer:4f31c02a96de`:

1. `agent_send` writes the message to the sender's durable queue with the
   `suzent_peer` transport.
2. The existing Devices grant supplies the peer URL and scoped bearer token.
3. The receiver acknowledges only after the message is committed to its own
   durable inbox.
4. The receiver wakes the authenticated peer's dedicated
   `suzent:<device_id>` session.

An offline peer is retried with bounded exponential backoff for up to 48
attempts. The sender can use `agent_read` to inspect the peer-owned session when
it comes back online, and `agent_stop` requests cooperative cancellation of that
session.

Remote callers cannot choose or inspect arbitrary local chat IDs. Optional
streaming session names are placed below their authenticated
`suzent:<device_id>:` namespace, while inbox/read/stop always operate on the
dedicated default session.


---

# Canvas (A2UI)

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/canvas




The **Canvas** is a structured UI layer that lets the agent render interactive components — tables, forms, cards, buttons, badges — directly in the Suzent interface, alongside the chat.

The agent calls `render_ui` to push a **surface** (a component tree) to the frontend. The user can interact with it (click buttons, submit forms), and those interactions are sent back to the agent as messages, creating a conversational UI loop.

## Concepts

### Surface

A surface is a named, renderable UI panel. It has:
- **`surface_id`** — a stable slug (e.g. `"search_results"`). Calling `render_ui` with the same id replaces the surface in place (upsert semantics).
- **`component`** — the root of a component tree (see below).
- **`title`** — optional display name shown in the canvas tab strip.
- **`target`** — where to render: `"inline"` (inside the chat message, default) or `"canvas"` (the side panel).

### Component Tree

Components are plain JSON objects with a `"type"` field. They nest recursively via `"children"` lists, whose entries are themselves component objects.

`component` must be a JSON **object**. The recursive A2UI union is validated server-side by `A2UISurface`, but the tool schema sent to providers is a flat, provider-neutral object schema (`suzent.a2ui.schema.component_tool_schema()`): recursive `$defs` are rejected by some providers, and an untyped parameter made models guess (Anthropic streamed the tree as a JSON string; Gemini sent `children: [0, 1]`). A string containing a JSON *object* is still accepted for compatibility and logged as deprecated; any other string is rejected with an explanation and is never treated as HTML or text. Validation errors come back as one line per problem with the field path. When adding a field to `suzent.a2ui.models`, add it to `suzent.a2ui.schema` too; `tests/tools/test_render_ui_schema.py` fails on drift.

**Container types** (have `children`):

| Type | Description | Key fields |
|------|-------------|------------|
| `card` | Titled panel with a black header bar | `title`, `children` |
| `stack` | Vertical group | `children`, `gap` (`sm`/`md`/`lg`) |
| `columns` | Side-by-side columns | `children`, `ratios` (list of flex weights) |

**Leaf types**:

| Type | Description | Key fields |
|------|-------------|------------|
| `text` | Paragraph or heading | `content` ⚠️, `variant` (`body`/`heading`/`subheading`/`caption`/`code`) |
| `badge` | Status chip | `label` ⚠️, `color` (`default`/`success`/`warning`/`error`/`info`) |
| `button` | Clickable action | `label` ⚠️, `action` ⚠️, `variant` (`primary`/`secondary`/`danger`), `context`, `disabled` |
| `table` | Data grid | `columns` (list of `{key, label}`), `rows` (list of dicts) |
| `form` | Input form | `action` ⚠️, `submit_label`, `fields` (list of `{name, label, type, required, placeholder, options, default}`) |
| `list` | Bullet or numbered list | `items` (list of strings), `ordered` |
| `progress` | Progress bar | `value` (0–100), `label` |
| `divider` | Horizontal rule | — |
| `html` | Free-form HTML in a sandboxed iframe | `html` ⚠️, `height` (optional, px) |

> ⚠️ **Common mistake:** Do not use `"text"` as a field name — it is not valid for any component. Use:
> - `"content"` for `text` components
> - `"label"` for `badge` and `button` components
>
> Always set `"action"` on buttons and forms so the agent can identify which interaction was triggered.

### Targets

| Target | Behaviour |
|--------|-----------|
| `"inline"` (default) | Embeds the component tree in the current chat message, under a slim header with **Open in side panel** and **Fullscreen** buttons. Persists in message history. |
| `"canvas"` | Renders in the side panel's Canvas tab and leaves a compact pointer card in the chat message to reopen it from. Auto-opens the side panel on the chat's first canvas surface. Use it only for a surface kept in view and updated while the conversation continues (live progress, a dashboard being iterated on). |

Popping an inline surface out copies it into the Canvas tab and focuses it; the inline copy stays where it is.

Layout surfaces for a narrow column (roughly 360–700px): the chat column and the side panel are both about that wide.

### Interaction Callbacks

When the user interacts with a surface, the action is sent back to the agent as a user message:

```
[canvas: <action>] "<button_label>"          # button click
[canvas: <action>] {"field": "value", ...}   # form submit
```

The `action` string is whatever you set in the component's `"action"` field. Always give buttons and forms distinct, descriptive action names.

## Usage

```python
render_ui(
    surface_id="results",
    title="Search Results",
    component={...},
    target="canvas",   # optional, default
)
```

### Example — card with status badges and buttons

```python
render_ui(
    surface_id="status",
    title="Analysis Status",
    component={
        "type": "card",
        "title": "WorldReasoner Results",
        "children": [
            {"type": "text", "content": "Evaluation complete."},
            {"type": "badge", "label": "92% Accuracy", "color": "success"},
            {"type": "badge", "label": "High Confidence", "color": "info"},
            {"type": "button", "label": "View Details", "action": "view_details"},
            {"type": "button", "label": "Export CSV", "action": "export_csv", "variant": "secondary"},
        ],
    }
)
```

### Example — data table

```python
render_ui(
    surface_id="llm_scores",
    title="LLM Benchmark Scores",
    component={
        "type": "table",
        "columns": [
            {"key": "model", "label": "Model"},
            {"key": "score", "label": "Score"},
            {"key": "category", "label": "Category"},
        ],
        "rows": [
            {"model": "Claude 3.5", "score": "92%", "category": "Reasoning"},
            {"model": "GPT-4o",    "score": "88%", "category": "Reasoning"},
        ],
    }
)
```

### Example — input form

```python
render_ui(
    surface_id="booking",
    title="Book a Table",
    component={
        "type": "form",
        "action": "confirm_booking",
        "submit_label": "Confirm",
        "fields": [
            {"name": "date",   "label": "Date",   "type": "text",   "required": True},
            {"name": "guests", "label": "Guests", "type": "number"},
            {"name": "notes",  "label": "Notes",  "type": "textarea"},
        ],
    }
)
# When submitted, agent receives: [canvas: confirm_booking] {"date": "...", "guests": 2, "notes": "..."}
```

### Example — inline quick-action panel

```python
render_ui(
    surface_id="quick_actions",
    target="inline",
    component={
        "type": "stack",
        "children": [
            {"type": "text", "content": "Choose an action:", "variant": "subheading"},
            {"type": "button", "label": "Run Deep Analysis", "action": "deep_analysis"},
            {"type": "button", "label": "Skip",              "action": "skip", "variant": "secondary"},
        ],
    }
)
```

### Example — multi-column layout

```python
render_ui(
    surface_id="dashboard",
    title="Dashboard",
    component={
        "type": "columns",
        "ratios": [2, 1],
        "children": [
            {
                "type": "card",
                "title": "Progress",
                "children": [
                    {"type": "progress", "label": "Data collection", "value": 80},
                    {"type": "progress", "label": "Analysis",        "value": 45},
                ],
            },
            {
                "type": "stack",
                "children": [
                    {"type": "badge", "label": "Running", "color": "warning"},
                    {"type": "button", "label": "Stop", "action": "stop_job", "variant": "danger"},
                ],
            },
        ],
    }
)
```

## Free-form HTML (`html` component)

### Shared presentation

Chat and Canvas share one live renderer per surface ID. `target` selects its
initial placement; moving it later changes its location without creating a
second renderer. The transcript keeps a compact pointer with “Show here” while
the surface is in Canvas. Fullscreen expands the existing sidebar using the
same state as dragging it across the chat; shrinking restores its docked width.
Opening fullscreen from chat first moves the surface to Canvas. Switching
Canvas tabs parks inactive renderers.

The shared provider is scoped to the chat. Connected DOM nodes move using
`Element.moveBefore` where supported, preserving iframe state as well as React
form state. Older webviews fall back to `appendChild`: React state survives,
but those engines may reload an iframe when reparenting it.

When the typed components can't express what you need — charts, SVG diagrams, custom dashboards, interactive prototypes — use the `html` component. It renders a self-contained HTML document in a **sandboxed iframe**.

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `html` | `str` | Self-contained HTML. May be a full document or a bare fragment. |
| `height` | `int \| None` | Fixed height in px. When omitted, the iframe **auto-sizes** to its content. |

Document-style HTML (news, reports, articles) should omit `height`. The resize
reporter measures the body independently of the iframe viewport, including
content changes, image loads and fonts, so it can grow past 4000px and shrink
when the panel widens. Canvas owns scrolling and its header stays outside the
scrollable body. A standalone HTML surface uses the document's own spacing,
without an extra iframe border or Canvas padding.

Viewport-based applications (maps, editors, dashboards) should set `height`.
For a standalone fixed-height HTML surface, Canvas limits the iframe to the
available panel height and leaves scrolling inside it. Nested fixed-height
HTML components retain their own scroll region within the surrounding document.

### Sandbox model

The HTML runs with `sandbox="allow-scripts"` (and **not** `allow-same-origin`):

- **Scripts run** — so charting libraries, animations, and interactive controls work.
- **Isolated from the host** — no access to the app's cookies, `localStorage`, or parent DOM. It cannot read or modify the rest of Suzent.

This is the same trust level Suzent uses to preview agent-authored `.html` files.

### Sending feedback back to the agent

Because the iframe is isolated, interactive HTML talks back to the agent via `postMessage`. Post a message to `window.parent` with this shape:

```js
window.parent.postMessage(
  { type: 'a2ui:action', action: 'my_action', context: { /* any JSON */ } },
  '*'
);
```

The host validates the message (shape + origin) and delivers it to the agent exactly like a button click or form submit:

```
[canvas: my_action] {"...": "..."}
```

So a button, chart click, or form inside your HTML can drive the conversation. Use distinct, descriptive `action` names just like with `button`/`form` components.

> The host also injects a tiny script that reports content height for auto-sizing. You don't need to add it — just emit your HTML.

### Example — HTML dashboard with a feedback button

```python
render_ui(
    surface_id="london_food_plan",
    title="London Food Plan",
    component={
        "type": "html",
        "html": """
            <div style="font-family: monospace; padding: 16px;">
              <h2>London Food Plan</h2>
              <p>Status: <strong>Ready to book</strong></p>
              <button onclick="
                window.parent.postMessage(
                  {type:'a2ui:action', action:'start_booking_bot',
                   context:{stage:'stage_2_reservations'}}, '*')
              ">Start Auto-Booking</button>
            </div>
        """,
    }
)
# When the button is clicked, the agent receives:
# [canvas: start_booking_bot] {"stage": "stage_2_reservations"}
```

### When to use `html` vs typed components

- Prefer **typed components** (`table`, `form`, `button`, …) for simple, structured UI that talks back — they're styled to match Suzent and validated by the schema.
- Reach for **`html`** when you need rich visuals or layouts the vocabulary can't express. Both render in the same canvas and support the same `{action, context}` feedback loop, so you can mix them across surfaces.

## Ask Question Tool

For collecting user input during a task, prefer `ask_question` over `render_ui`. It blocks the agent until the user responds, then returns the answers as structured data.

```python
ask_question(questions=[
    QuestionItem(question="What's your goal?", options=["Build a feature", "Fix a bug", "Refactor"], required=True),
    QuestionItem(question="Any additional context?"),
])
# Returns: User answered: {"what_s_your_goal": "Fix a bug", "any_additional_context": "..."}
```

### Rendering Behaviour

Every call renders as a paged form, one question per page:

| Shape | Field |
|-------|-------|
| `options`, no `multi_select` | Single-select list |
| `options` + `multi_select=True` | Checkbox list |
| No `options` | Free-text `textarea` |

### QuestionItem Fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `question` | `str` | The question text |
| `options` | `list[str] \| None` | Selectable choices |
| `multi_select` | `bool` | Allow multiple selections (checkbox list) |
| `field_name` | `str` | Response key (auto-slugged from question if omitted) |
| `required` | `bool` | Mark the field required |

### Paged Form UX

When rendered as a form, `ask_question` shows one question at a time with **Back**, **Skip**, and **Next/Submit** navigation. The user can skip optional questions; **Next** is only enabled once the current field has a value.

Every `select` and `multiselect` field ends with a "Type something else…" item, which expands a text input on the same page. Each question keeps its own free-text state, so moving to the next page starts empty.

Keyboard: number keys `1`–`9` pick (or toggle) the option with that badge, including the "something else" item; `Enter` moves to the next question or submits (`Shift+Enter` adds a newline in a textarea); `Esc` leaves the free-text input so number keys work again.

### Callback

- Form submit → `[canvas: submit_question] {"field": "value", ...}`
  - Single-select → `string`; multi-select → `list[str]`; textarea → `string`

## Canvas Persistence

Canvas surfaces are persisted to `localStorage` keyed by chat ID. They survive page reloads and are restored when switching back to a conversation.

## Upsert Semantics

Calling `render_ui` with the same `surface_id` **replaces** the existing surface. There is no `remove_ui` — to clear a surface, replace it with an empty stack or stop sending updates.

- In the Canvas tab, the surface is replaced in place.
- Within one turn, the inline part is replaced in place, so live progress updates rather than stacking copies.
- Across turns, the new version renders at the latest message. Every render carries a `rev` (milliseconds, stamped by `render_ui`), and an inline copy collapses to a one-line "updated later" row with a **Show** toggle once a copy of the same id with a larger `rev` is mounted. Copies saved before `rev` existed never collapse.


---

# Chat Storage

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/chat-storage




Each chat's append-only JSONL event log is its source of truth. `chats.db` is an
index of the logs: the `chats` table and its full-text search rows are what the
sidebar, search and every `get_chat` read, and they can be rebuilt from the logs
at any time. What is still planned is in the [roadmap](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/roadmap#chat-storage).

## Display history and model context

These are separate records. The model context may be summarized or trimmed;
the visible conversation is captured from the AG-UI stream (text, reasoning,
tools, approvals, citations and inline surfaces). The run UUID identifies the
assistant record, so repeating a prompt such as “continue” does not match an
older answer. Finalization updates that run's record in place.

The quick snapshot commits the captured output and model state together, before
background post-processing. Post-processing preserves the display timeline and
does not reconstruct it from compacted model messages. Failed and stopped runs
retain whatever output was actually received; an earlier answer is not used as
a substitute. Legacy history rebuilding remains available for callers without
a captured stream identity.

During a run, transient drafts still live in SQLite rather than the JSONL log.
The completed, stopped or failed run's quick snapshot makes its captured output
durable in JSONL. An abrupt process exit before that snapshot can therefore
leave only a SQLite draft of the latest partial output.

## Where chats live

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `<data>/chats/<chat_id>.jsonl` | The chat's event log. Authoritative. |
| `<data>/chats/.media/<sha256>` | Strings of 64 KiB or more from any log (pasted images, large tool output), stored once by content hash. |
| `<data>/chats/.trash/` | Logs of deleted chats, renamed `<chat_id>.<utc timestamp>.jsonl`, purged after 30 days. |
| `<data>/chats/.corrupt/` | Logs that could not be read, set aside for inspection. |
| `<data>/chats.db` | The `chats` row of each chat, its search rows, and `chat_log_index`: the `seq`, size and mtime of each log as of its last commit. |

The log directory is named after the database file, so a test database at
`/tmp/abc.db` keeps its logs in `/tmp/abc/`. File names are the percent-encoded
chat id, so a peer chat `suzent:<peer>` lives in `suzent%3A<peer>.jsonl`.

## Event format

Each line is one event. Most lines are one message, as in Codex CLI and Claude
Code transcripts:

```json
{"v": 1, "seq": 7, "ts": "2026-10-17T16:00:00+00:00", "type": "message.append", "data": {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}}
```

`seq` increases by one per event within a file. Folding the events in order with
`apply_event` (`src/suzent/database/chat_log.py`) yields the chat's *projection*:
the JSON form of its row that `project_chat` produces, plus its retry
checkpoint, which has no row.

| `type` | `data` |
|---|---|
| `chat.created` / `chat.imported` | The projection with both lists empty; their items follow as appends. `imported` marks a chat that existed before its log. |
| `meta.set` | Changed values among `title`, `pinned`, `project_id`, `working_directory`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `last_active_at`, `turn_count`, `context_usage`. |
| `config.merge` | `{"set": {...}, "unset": [...]}` for changed config keys. |
| `message.append` | One display message added at the end. |
| `messages.splice` | `{"start", "delete", "insert"}` applied to the display messages, for any change other than appending. |
| `state.set` | Changed fields of the agent state other than its history: `kind` (`none`, `empty`, `json`, `raw`), `meta` (`version`, `model_id`, `tool_names`) and `raw` (base64, for state that is not the JSON format). |
| `history.append` | One pydantic-ai message added at the end of the history. |
| `history.splice` | A splice applied to the history, for any change other than appending. |
| `checkpoint.set` | The retry checkpoint for the coming turn (see below). |
| `checkpoint.update` | `{"id", "set"}`: fields of that checkpoint, ignored if a newer checkpoint replaced it. |
| `chat.deleted` | Empty. The file then moves to `.trash/`. |

Anywhere in `data`, a string of 64 KiB or more is written as
`{"$media": "<sha256>"}` and read back from `.media/`.

Revision counters (`state_revision`, `finalized_revision`, `state_stage`,
`state_updated_at`) and `last_result_at` are not logged: they coordinate the
running process rather than describe the conversation, and a rebuilt row starts
them at zero. Streaming drafts (display rows with `_streaming_draft`) are not
logged either, since the turn's real write replaces them; the draft write
commits to SQLite alone.

## How a write works

Every write to a `chats` row ends in `commit_chat_changes(session, chat_ids)`
instead of `session.commit()`. That includes the methods on
`ChatOperationsMixin`, project moves, and the writes elsewhere that edit a row
directly (heartbeat config, the heartbeat route, the turn-end file snapshot).

1. The session flushes its changes to SQLite without committing, which takes
   SQLite's write lock.
2. The chat's in-process lock is taken.
3. The uncommitted row is projected and compared with the log's projection,
   which `ChatEventLog` keeps for the 64 most recent chats. Lists are diffed by
   common prefix and suffix: items added at the end become one append event
   each, and any other change (a compaction, a rollback, a retry) is one
   splice. The log grows with the conversation, not with the number of writes.
4. The events are appended and fsynced, and `chat_log_index` is updated in the
   same SQLite transaction.
5. SQLite commits. If the commit fails, the log is truncated back to its old
   size; if the process dies first, the log is ahead of SQLite.

Because the difference is taken against the row, a write that reached the row
some other way is recorded by the next logged write to that chat.

## Starting up

`ChatDatabase.__init__` runs `reconcile_chat_logs()` after the migrations and
before anything can write. It compares every log's size and mtime with
`chat_log_index` and replays only the logs that differ, so its cost is one
`stat` per chat when nothing went wrong. A replay folds the log and rewrites the
row from it when they disagree:

- events a crash kept out of SQLite are applied;
- a log ending in `chat.deleted` deletes the row and moves to `.trash/`;
- a hand-edited log is applied;
- a `chats.db` that was deleted comes back, because an empty index matches no
  log. Projects live only in `chats.db`, so a chat whose project no longer
  exists joins the default project, and the move is logged.

A crash mid-append can leave a partial final line. Readers ignore everything
after the last newline, and the next append truncates it first. A log that
cannot be read at all moves to `.corrupt/`, and the chat's next write starts a
new log from its row.

The server then runs `import_unlogged_chats()` in a background thread. It gives
every chat without a log a `chat.imported` event, and moves the checkpoints of
the old `retry_checkpoints` table into the logs before dropping it. A chat
written before the import reaches it gets its `chat.imported` from that write.

## Retry checkpoints

`save_retry_checkpoint` runs at the start of a turn. When the state it is given
is the chat as stored, which is the normal case, the checkpoint's `before` is
`{"seq": n}`: the position of the event just before it. Only a checkpoint that
differs from the stored chat carries a copy of the messages and state. A retry
folds the log up to `n` to get the state it restores, then writes that state as
an ordinary rewrite, so the log keeps every turn that was retried away.

## Commands

```bash
suzent chats show <chat_id>  # print the conversation the log holds
suzent chats verify          # fold every log, compare it with its row, exit 1 on any difference
suzent chats rebuild-index   # rewrite every row from its log; stop the server first
```

## Compaction failure and concurrency

Compaction rewrites the model context, while streamed display rows remain the
conversation timeline. An empty summary, an incomplete chunk, or a timeout must
not replace context with a placeholder or discard the unsummarized middle.
Automatic compaction keeps the input history on failure; when the estimated
request already fills the context window it raises an error instead of sending
that request. Summaries that do not reduce the history's estimated token count
are skipped. Token estimates are approximate and do not guarantee provider
acceptance.

The retained tail begins at a safe tool-call boundary. The latest real user
prompt is also retained when it falls outside that tail, including its image or
file parts. Summary requests distinguish user text from tool results. Chunk
summaries are limited to three concurrent calls, and every chunk must succeed
before a merged summary can replace context.

Manual `/compact` uses the configured compaction timeout and commits against the
revision read before summarization. If a newer snapshot has committed meanwhile,
it reports a skipped result and preserves that newer state. Complete, skipped,
and error events terminate the frontend's compaction indicator.

[Pydantic AI Harness compaction](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/compaction/)
provides reusable model-context strategies, including incremental summarization,
user-message retention and tool-pair preservation. Suzent currently uses its own
history processor; those strategies do not replace its display log or revision
checks. The installed Harness 0.24.0 differs from the current online API (for
example, it lacks `compact_now`), so adopting it requires a version-specific
integration and regression tests.


---

# Focal Agent (Suzent Regent)

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/focal-agent




The Focal Agent is the singleton chat shown to users as **Suzent Regent**, or
**Regent** in the app. It sees every project, dispatches work to project
sessions, and is woken when one of them blocks on the user or finishes. It never
does project work itself. The code calls it "focal" throughout
(`suzent.core.focal_agent`); user-facing and model-facing text calls it Regent.

It was first shown as SUZENT. Existing installs pick up the new name without a
migration: the pinned title is restored on every `get_or_create_focal_chat()`,
and an untouched `heartbeat.md` or notes skeleton from then is upgraded through
`_PREVIOUS_FOCAL_HEARTBEATS` and `_PREVIOUS_FOCAL_NOTES`. The hidden project
keeps whatever name it was created with.

## Identity and storage

- One chat with the fixed ID `focal-suzent`, created on first use by
  `get_or_create_focal_chat()`. `is_focal_chat()` also accepts a chat whose
  config has `is_focal_agent: true` or `platform: "focal"`.
- It lives in the hidden system project `suzent-focal` (in
  `HIDDEN_PROJECT_SLUGS`), whose folder holds its `heartbeat.md`.
- Its title is pinned to `Regent`; auto-title skips it and
  `get_or_create_focal_chat()` restores the name if it changed.

## Tool policy

`apply_focal_tool_policy()` runs in `chat_processor` before every Focal turn
and overrides whatever the request asked for:

- `tools` is set to `FOCAL_TOOL_NAMES`: agent list/read/stop,
  `FocalDispatchTool`, web search and fetch, memory and session search,
  ask-question, skills, read-only file tools, `FocalScheduleTool`, and
  `FocalNotesTool`. The plain
  `AgentSendTool` is not in the set.
- Every other registered tool goes into `denied_tools`. Unequipped tools would
  otherwise still be reachable through ToolSearch.
- MCP is disabled, and `cwd` and `sandbox_volumes` are removed: project
  sessions carry their own working directory.
- `permission_mode` is `full_access`, since nothing in the set changes state
  outside Suzent.

Focal-only behavior lives in Focal-only tools, so other agents' schemas never
carry it. They sit together in `suzent.tools.focal`: `FocalDispatchTool`
(`agent_dispatch`, a subclass of `AgentSendTool`), `FocalScheduleTool`
(`schedule_wakeup`, a subclass of `ScheduleTool`) and `FocalNotesTool`
(`update_notes`). The two subclasses call their parents' internals, so a change
to `AgentSendTool._deliver` or `ScheduleTool`'s helpers needs a look there too.
All three have an empty `group` and are
not deferrable, so no other chat can equip or discover them, and all refuse
any chat that is not the Focal Agent. Their descriptions say "you" rather than
naming the Focal Agent, so nothing Regent reads calls it anything but Regent.

They need runtime names of their own: `is_denied()` resolves a runtime name to
one class through the registry, so a shared `agent_send` would be checked
against whichever class won the mapping.

## Global context

The `inject_focal_context` prompt layer (runtime) adds
`build_focal_global_context()` to Focal turns only: every non-archived project
with its id and slug, up to 10 sessions per project, and each session's tasks.
Sessions come from the project's tasks plus any chat in the project that is
running now, plus the 20 most recent sessions Regent started
(`parent_chat_id`), which may have no task. ACP sessions never do. Sessions
with work waiting on the user sort first, then running ones, and ACP sessions
are marked with their agent. Any other chat with no tasks that is not running
is not listed.

Each project line ends with one line from that project's `context.md`, read
live by `_project_overview()`: the first line of its Overview section, else its
first line of prose, cut at 160 characters. That gives Regent what each project
is about without a copy that could drift.

## Notes

Regent's notes are the `context.md` of `suzent-focal`, which core memory already
loads as the Context block for any chat in that project. Other chats keep their
project's `context.md` with the file tools; Regent has none, so
`FocalNotesTool` (`update_notes`) edits that one file and nothing else: an exact
`old_text` replacement, an entry added at the end of a `section` (created if
missing), or a plain append, capped at
`MAX_NOTES_CHARS` (8,000, where core memory starts truncating the block). An
edit reaches later turns as a core-memory diff reminder, like any other
context.md change.

`get_or_create_focal_chat()` seeds the file with `DEFAULT_FOCAL_NOTES`, a title
and empty sections, whenever it is missing. An existing file, even an empty
one, is left alone.

Regent has no library: it does no project work, so it produces no deliverables,
and `suzent-focal/` holds only its notes and `heartbeat.md`. Project knowledge
stays in each project's own `context.md`, maintained by that project's
sessions.

`format_core_memory_section()` swaps the "How to update your memory" lines for
the Focal chat: point at `update_notes`, and keep project and task status out,
since `build_focal_global_context()` supplies it fresh each turn. The tool's
`session_guidance` says what belongs in the notes.

## Dispatch

Both paths go through `FocalDispatchTool` and the
[agent inbox](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/agent-inbox). It has no `wait` parameter and refuses
external A2A agents: Regent never holds a turn open on another agent, which
would also hold back the wake-ups and reports queued behind it.

- **Existing session:** `agent_dispatch(agent_id=<chat id>, message=...)`.
  `watch_session()` sets `focal_watching` on the target so Focal hears when it
  finishes.
- **New session:** `agent_dispatch(agent_id="new", project_id=..., title=...,
  task_title=..., message=...)`. It creates
  a chat in the project with `permission_mode: "auto"` (Smart),
  `parent_chat_id` and `spawned_by_focal`, binds an `in_progress` task when
  `task_title` is given, and enqueues the message. The desktop renders that
  first `system_triggered` message as a user message (`focalRequestText`), so
  the session shows what it was asked.
- **New ACP session:** the same call with `acp_agent_id` (from
  `agent_list(status="acp")`, which tells Regent to use `agent_dispatch` rather
  than `agent`). The chat gets `runtime: "acp"` and `acp_agent_id`, so the inbox
  delivers through `run_acp_turn_text()` with the project folder as its
  working directory. Its `permission_mode` is `default`, not `auto`: for ACP,
  `auto` allows every request outright (`acp/permissions.py`), with no reviewer
  behind it. The inbox runs each ACP turn on a background stream, as ACP
  sub-agents do, so opening the session attaches to it and shows any pending
  approval. A request nobody answers fails closed after the broker's timeout.
  If the turn fails before saying anything (the agent isn't signed in, the
  handshake fails), `run_acp_turn_text(errors_out=...)` hands the inbox the
  `RUN_ERROR`, and the reply becomes "The ACP agent could not run this: …".
  Otherwise the empty reply would be dropped and Regent would never hear.
  `task_title` is refused, because an ACP agent can't update Suzent tasks and
  the task would stay `in_progress`, and the heartbeat would flag it as stalled.
  An unknown or uninstalled agent is refused before anything is created.
- **Paired Suzent:** `agent_dispatch(agent_id="peer:...")` goes through the
  peer outbox in `_deliver()`, asynchronously like any other message.

## Hearing back

Three events enqueue an inbox message to `focal-suzent`:

| Event | Source | Inbox `kind` |
|---|---|---|
| A session answers a message Focal sent it | `route_focal_reply()` from the inbox worker; replies over 4,000 characters are truncated | `agent_message` |
| A task becomes blocked on `user` or `error`, or its reason changes | `notify_focal_of_blocked_task()` from `TaskUpdateTool` | `task_blocked_notification` |
| A followed session closes its last open task | `notify_focal_of_finished_session()` from `TaskUpdateTool`, skipped while a Focal request to it is still in flight | `session_finished_notification` |

Any session may also message Regent itself with `agent_send`
(`_sendable_agent()`), but `agent_read` and `agent_stop` don't reach it: its
conversation spans every project.

A session counts as followed when Focal started it (`parent_chat_id`) or sent
it work (`focal_watching`). Blocked-task notices go to Focal for any session,
but only once the Focal chat exists; they never create it for a user who has
not opened Regent, except for sessions Focal started.

When a woken Focal turn replies, `announce_focal_reply()` also queues a
desktop notification, since the user may not have the chat open.

The global context tells Regent to filter rather than relay: blockers first,
one line each, no restated reports, and the quiet token (`HEARTBEAT_OK`) when a
session's reply or finish needs nothing from the user. A quiet reply is not
rolled back: the event and the reply stay in Regent's history, so it can still
answer what happened. It only reaches nobody: `announce_focal_reply()` skips
the notification, and `_persist_state` finalizes with `count_unread=False`, so
the unread badge stays put. The one exception is `task_blocked_notification`:
if Regent goes quiet on a blocker anyway, the notification carries the blocker
text itself. The desktop renders a quiet reply as "Nothing needed from you"
(`lib/quietReply.ts`, mirroring `is_quiet_reply()`).

## Heartbeat

The first `get_or_create_focal_chat()` enables the heartbeat at 30 minutes
and seeds `heartbeat.md` with `DEFAULT_FOCAL_HEARTBEAT`, once
(`focal_heartbeat_initialized`). After that the setting belongs to the user.
A checklist still identical to an earlier built-in one
(`_PREVIOUS_FOCAL_HEARTBEATS`) is upgraded in place; an edited one is never
touched.

To keep a quiet heartbeat free, `should_run_focal_heartbeat()` decides in code
before any model call:

- A user-edited checklist always runs.
- The default checklist runs only when `_heartbeat_findings()` is non-empty
  and its SHA-256 signature differs from `focal_heartbeat_signature`. Findings
  are sessions idle for 30 minutes with open tasks and nothing waiting on the
  user (`STALL_AFTER`), and blockers unanswered for 2 hours
  (`REMIND_BLOCKED_AFTER`).
- A skipped run is recorded as run (`record_skipped_heartbeat()`), so the
  schedule advances a full interval.

The signature is written by `record_focal_heartbeat_done()` only after a
check-in turn succeeds, so a failed or preempted check-in raises the same
findings next time.

A quiet check-in is rolled back only if it did nothing. `turn_acted()` looks
for any tool call outside the look-up tools (`_OBSERVING_TOOL_NAMES`): a
check-in that dispatched a nudge and then answered `HEARTBEAT_OK` stays in
history, unannounced, so Regent doesn't forget the nudge and send it again.
This holds for every chat's heartbeat, not only Regent's.

## Wake-ups

`schedule_wakeup` creates agent-sourced cron jobs on the Focal chat, at most
20. `kind="reminder"` always notifies; `kind="check"` sets `suppress_ok`, so
the user hears only when there is something to say. Focal wake-ups always run
inside the Focal chat under its own tool policy: there is no isolated variant,
which would run with a full tool set.

## Chat status

Each ordinary project chat (not Regent, sub-agents, chat apps or dreams; see
`is_tracked()` in `core/chat_status.py`) has one of four states. The user owns
only `resolved`; the rest are read from what the chat is doing. Tasks stay the
agent's own bookkeeping and never set the state directly except through the
waits below.

| State | Read from |
|---|---|
| `waiting` | An `ask_question` form held open (`a2ui.pending.chats_waiting()`), a pending tool approval (`config._pending_approvals`), a task `blocked` on `user` or `error`, or the Decision model's read of the last reply |
| `running` | A turn in progress (`running_chat_ids()`) |
| `resolved` | The user resolved it (`POST /chats/{id}/resolved`) |
| `idle` | None of the above |

`chat_state()` decides in that order, except that a held question or approval
beats running (the run is parked on the user), and resolving beats waits read
from tasks or replies.

- **When a turn starts** (not a heartbeat), `begin_turn()` numbers it and
  clears `resolved_at` and the last judgement.
- **After each turn** that is not a heartbeat, failed or was cancelled,
  `schedule_judgement()` runs `judge_turn()` in the background on the
  `decision` role. The answer is parsed strictly (`TurnJudgement`) into
  `waiting_on_user`, a short `reason` and a one-line `summary`, saved in the
  `chat_status` table. A failure or unreadable answer keeps the previous record,
  and a judgement whose turn a newer one has overtaken is dropped.
- Both hooks run in `ChatProcessor.process_turn()` and in
  `acp.runtime.stream_acp_turn()`, so chats on an ACP agent are tracked the
  same way.
- Changes emit a `chat_status_changed` bus event.
- `list_chat_states()` lists waiting and running chats of any age, and idle or
  resolved ones active in the last seven days. It queries the projects'
  chats directly (`list_board_chats()`), with no cap on how many it scans. `focal_status()` counts waiting
  chats from it.

## HTTP API

| Route | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET /focal` | Create the chat if needed and return `focal_status()`: waiting chats, stalled sessions and auto-running counts, chats per state, per-project and per-chat waiting counts, unread count and last message |
| `GET /focal/chats` | `list_chat_states()` with per-state counts; `?project_id=` narrows it to one project, and `?chat_id=` returns that one chat however long it has been quiet |
| `POST /chats/{id}/resolved` | Body `{"resolved": bool}`: resolve the chat for the user, or reopen it |
| `GET /focal/panel` | The fixed tool list and scheduled wake-ups, for the Tools tab |
| `DELETE /focal/wakeups/{job_id}` | Cancel one of Focal's own wake-ups; any other job id is refused |

## Desktop

- `FocalAgentCard` at the top of the sidebar, fed by `useFocalStatus`.
- `FocalAgentCard` sits above the sidebar's navigation, like a pinned contact.
- On the Focal chat the sidebar card becomes a profile (`regent-card-hero`):
  the flat mark gives way to a 56px `RegentCube` that grows in, and `ChatList`
  marks the navigation and project sections `regent-dimmed` (they return to
  full strength on hover or focus).
- The header keeps its single `h-12` row and every icon in place.
  `ConversationIdentity` renders `LiveRegentIdentity`: "SUZENT Regent" and a
  pill for working, waiting or stalled. While the left sidebar is collapsed,
  `LiveRegentLogo` replaces the `SuzentLogo` in the sidebar trigger slot, so the
  cube appears exactly where the logo was. Both read "working" from the chat's
  own stream as well as from status (`components/regent/RegentHeader.tsx`).
- Regent's replies are signed with its mark (`AssistantMessage`'s `regent`):
  the live badge shows `RegentMark` through `AgentBadge`'s `icon`, scanning
  while it works, and past replies carry the small mark and "Regent".
- `FocalBriefing` is only the greeting on an empty chat; the header carries the
  name and what waits on the user.
- Regent has two marks in `components/regent/`: `RegentMark`, the flat Suzent
  head under a floating circlet, for the sidebar row and reply badges; and `RegentCube`, the
  greeting cube wearing the circlet, for the open profile and the header's logo
  slot. Both take a `RegentState` from
  `regentState()`: `working` while Regent runs (cube turns, eyes scan, circlet
  lifts), `waiting` when something waits on the user (gem pulses orange), else
  `idle`. `useRegentNod()` replays a one-off nod when a new message arrives.
  All of it stops under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- The Tasks panel on the Focal chat shows the all-projects board grouped by
  session, with a remembered project filter.
- The Tools tab shows `FocalToolsPanel` instead of the tool picker, and the
  input hides the folder and attachment controls.

# Memory Architecture

Source: https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/memory-architecture




How memory is written, consolidated, indexed, and read.
Companions: [Memory](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/features/memory#how-memory-is-tidied) for how the dream
behaves from the outside, [Memory internals](https://suzent.com/zh-Hans/docs/developing/architecture/memory-internals) for the class-by-class reference.

## Three tiers, one job each

| tier | location | job | who writes it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capture buffer | `sandbox/shared/memory/archive/YYYY-MM-DD.md` | Lossless and fast. Never reasoned over at write time. | write path, append only |
| Knowledge base | `~/.suzent/notebook/**/*.md` | Consolidated claims with provenance and lifecycle | the dream, via file tools |
| Search index | `~/.suzent/memory` (LanceDB) | Derived. Rebuilt per file, never authored. | the indexer, exclusively |

The direction of travel is one-way: logs feed the vault, both feed the index, and the
index feeds retrieval. Nothing reads back up the chain.

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'neutral'}}%%
flowchart LR
    subgraph capture["Capture"]
        LOG[("archive/<br/>YYYY-MM-DD.md")]
    end
    subgraph knowledge["Knowledge"]
        VAULT[("notebook/<br/>vault pages")]
        STATE[".state/<br/>tombstones · superseded<br/>dream_state"]
    end
    subgraph derived["Derived"]
        DB[("LanceDB<br/>archival_memories<br/>memory_blocks")]
    end

    TURN["chat turn"] --> WRITE["write path"]
    WRITE -->|append| LOG
    LOG -->|read-only| DREAM["dream"]
    DREAM -->|create / update| VAULT
    DREAM -->|hand-off| STATE
    LOG --> IDX["indexer"]
    VAULT --> IDX
    STATE -->|filter| IDX
    IDX -->|delete-then-add| DB
    DB --> RECALL["retrieval"]
    RECALL --> TURN
```

## Write path, in batches of turns

Extraction reads each chat's event log, the same one the chat is rebuilt from, so there
is no separate copy to drift. `memory/extraction_queue.py` keeps a cursor per chat in
`.memory_cursors.json` next to the log; a cursor is the `(event seq, index)` of the last
message extracted, because one splice event can insert several messages. The turns past
it are extracted:

- at the end of a turn, when 6 or more turns or 8k characters are pending;
- otherwise when the chat has been quiet for 10 minutes;
- before the chat's context is compacted, so compacted turns stay recallable;
- on start, for anything still pending when the app last closed.

A batch (at most 16k characters) is the new turns, each dated with when it happened,
after the last two already-extracted turns marked as context only. It goes through
`MemoryManager.process_conversation_for_memories`. The cursor moves only once the batch
is written, and a failed extraction raises, so the turns stay queued and are retried.
With no cursor file, every existing chat starts at its current end, except for the turns
the old transcript-based queue still had pending; those are carried over by counting
trailing turns. Turns from a chat with memory switched off, and chats the app runs for
itself (the organizer, subagents), are skipped rather than queued.

Each turn in a batch is the user's message with hidden reminders stripped, the tool
calls made this turn with the start of each result, and the final reply. The main
agent's system prompt and reminders are left out on purpose: the reminder carries
recalled memories, and an extractor that saw them would store them again. Tool calls
answered before the turn started are excluded, because the history snapshot spans the
whole chat.

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme':'neutral'}}%%
flowchart TD
    A["turn text"] --> B["recall 10 nearest known facts<br/>(best-effort — failure means<br/>extraction runs as before)"]
    B --> C["typed capture + gate<br/>prompt carries 'already in memory'"]
    C -->|nothing kept| Z["stop"]
    C --> D["append to today's log"]
    D --> E["reindex_file_now(archive, today)"]
    E --> F[("LanceDB")]
```

There is deliberately **no write-time deduplication**. A 0.85 cosine threshold used to
sit here and silently dropped *updates* to facts (#34). Repetition is suppressed one step
earlier instead — the extractor is shown what memory already holds and told that a fact
which *changes* a known one must still be emitted.

## Typed capture

Extraction is `memory/capture.py`: the model proposes at most `MAX_CANDIDATES` (5) candidates per
batch, each labelled with

- `kind`: `user` (about the person), `experience` (a lesson from how a task went) or
  `world` (a fact read in a file, page or tool result);
- `source`: `user_said`, `user_did`, `outcome`, `agent_said` or `tool_output`;
- `horizon`: `durable`, `dated` or `ephemeral`;
- `evidence`: the exact words behind it.

A deterministic gate then drops what the labels prove is not a memory. Its drop codes:

| code | dropped because |
| --- | --- |
| `agent_said` | the agent's own words are not evidence |
| `ephemeral` | only matters for the current task |
| `user_kind_wrong_source` | a User fact must come from `user_said` / `user_did` |
| `evidence_not_in_user_line` | the evidence is not in any USER line of the new turns (≥0.8 bigram overlap) |
| `tool_output_without_citation` | tool output that is not a World fact, or has no path or URL |
| `outcome_not_experience` | an outcome filed as something other than Experience |
| `experience_channel` | a lesson; only the experience step below proposes those |
| `context_free_choice` | a pick that only makes sense inside the chat ("option 2", "the second one") |
| `rejected` | matches `.state/rejected.jsonl` |
| `restatement` | ≥0.9 similar to a fact already in the recall set |
| `over_cap` | past the per-batch cap |

Kept facts go to the daily log as before, with tags (`kind:` `source:`, `dated
stale_after:<+90 days>`, `ungrounded` when a specific is not in the evidence) and a
`> "evidence"` line under the fact, which the dream reads.

Every drop, with its code and the full candidate, is appended to
`.state/capture_dropped.jsonl` as `{"ts", "chat_id", "channel": "facts", "dropped"}`, so a
wrongly dropped fact can be found and the gate tuned. This replaced an untyped extractor
that wrote whatever looked like a fact; a replay of past batches showed it storing the
agent's own words and task specs as facts about the user, so it was removed rather than
kept as an option.

Scheduled turns are filtered per turn in `extraction_queue._is_scheduled`, so a cron or
heartbeat run inside a normal chat is not captured as user facts. `cron` is deliberately
not in `_is_system_chat`: that list also makes a chat stateless.

### Experience capture
